title: Translational kinetic energy
body: K=\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}
caution: For a change in kinetic energy, use \Delta K=\tfrac12 m\left(v_f^{2}-v_i^{2}\right), not \tfrac12 m(\Delta v)^2.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.1 "An object's translational kinetic energy is given by the equation K = 1/2 mv^2"

title: Kinetic energy is a scalar and depends on the observer's frame
body: Translational kinetic energy is a scalar, and observers in different frames of reference may measure different values for the same object.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.2, 3.1.A.3 "Different observers may measure different values of the translational kinetic energy"

title: Work done by a constant force
body: W=F_{\parallel}d=Fd\cos\theta
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.3.i "Only the component of the force exerted on a system that is parallel to the displacement ... will change the system's total energy"

title: Work is a signed scalar; only the parallel component changes energy
body: Work is a scalar that may be positive, negative, or zero, and a force component perpendicular to the displacement changes the direction of motion without changing kinetic energy.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.2 "Work is a scalar quantity that may be positive, negative, or zero"; 3.2.A.3.ii

title: Sign of work: positive when done on the system
body: Positive work is work done on the system, which transfers energy into the system; negative work transfers energy out.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 "Work is the amount of energy transferred into or out of a system by a force exerted on that system"

title: Work-energy theorem
body: \Delta K=\sum_i W_i=\sum_i F_{\parallel,i}\,d
caution: Write \Delta K=\tfrac12 m\left(v_f^{2}-v_i^{2}\right); do not write \tfrac12 m(\Delta v)^2.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.4 "the change in an object's kinetic energy is equal to the sum of the work (net work) being done by all forces"

title: Work from a force-displacement graph
body: Work equals the area under the curve of a graph of F (parallel component) as a function of displacement.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.5 "Work is equal to the area under the curve of a graph of F as a function of displacement"

title: Conservative force
body: A conservative force does work that is path-independent, depends only on the initial and final configurations of the system, and is zero if the system returns to its initial configuration.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.i "The work done by a conservative force exerted on a system is path-independent"; 3.2.A.1.ii

title: Nonconservative force
body: A nonconservative force does work that is path-dependent, and no potential energy is associated with it.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.iv "The work done by a nonconservative force is path-dependent"; 3.2.A.1.iii

title: CED examples of nonconservative forces
body: The CED names two examples of nonconservative forces.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1.v "Examples of nonconservative forces are friction and air resistance"

title: Energy dissipated by friction
body: E_{\text{dissipated}}=F_{f}\,d_{\text{path}}
caution: d_path is the length of the path over which friction acts, not the net displacement.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.4.iii "The energy dissipated by friction is typically equated to the force of friction times the length of the path"

title: Potential energy of a system
body: A system of two or more objects has potential energy only if its objects interact through conservative forces; it is a scalar associated with the positions of the objects in the system.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1, 3.3.A.2 "Potential energy is a scalar quantity associated with the position of objects within a system"

title: Zero of potential energy is the observer's choice
body: The definition of zero potential energy for a system is a decision made by the observer to simplify analysis.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.3 "The definition of zero potential energy for a given system is a decision made by the observer"

title: Elastic potential energy of an ideal spring
body: U_s=\tfrac{1}{2}k\,(\Delta x)^{2}
caution: \Delta x is the stretch or compression from the spring's equilibrium length.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.4.i "The elastic potential energy of an ideal spring"

title: General gravitational potential energy of two spherical masses
body: U_g=-\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r}

title: Change in gravitational PE near a planet's surface
body: \Delta U_g=mg\,\Delta y
caution: This is an approximation valid because g is nearly constant near the surface.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.4.iii "the change in gravitational potential energy ... may be approximated by the equation"

title: Total potential energy of a multi-object system
body: The total potential energy of a system with more than two objects is the sum of the potential energy of each pair of objects.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.5 "the sum of the potential energy of each pair of objects within the system"

title: Which energies a system can have
body: A system of a single object can have only kinetic energy; potential energy requires objects interacting via conservative forces or a reversible change of shape.
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.1 "A system composed of only a single object can only have kinetic energy"; 3.4.A.2

title: Mechanical energy
body: E_{\text{mech}}=K+U
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.1 "Mechanical energy is the sum of a system's kinetic and potential energies"

title: Conservation of energy and system choice
body: If the work done on the selected system is zero and there are no nonconservative interactions within it, mechanical energy is constant; if the work is nonzero, energy is transferred between the system and its environment, and the change in total energy equals the energy transferred in or out.
caution: State which system you chose, since the choice determines whether its energy changes.
ced_evidence: 3.4.C.2, 3.4.C.3, 3.4.B.4 "that change will be equivalent to the energy transferred into or out of the system"

title: Energy changes within a system must balance
body: Any change to one type of energy in a system must be balanced by an equivalent change in other types within the system or by a transfer between the system and its surroundings.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.2 "Any change to a type of energy within a system must be balanced by an equivalent change"

title: Nonconservative forces dissipate mechanical energy
body: Nonconservative forces can dissipate mechanical energy as thermal energy or sound, though energy is conserved in all interactions.
ced_evidence: Boundary statement "mechanical energy can be dissipated as thermal energy or sound by nonconservative forces"; 3.4.C.1

title: Average power from energy
body: P_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.2 "Average power is the amount of energy being transferred or converted, divided by the time"

title: Average power from work
body: P_{\text{avg}}=\frac{W}{\Delta t}
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.3 "average power is the total work done, divided by the time during which that work was done"

title: Instantaneous power of a constant force
body: P=F_{\parallel}v=Fv\cos\theta
caution: This applies to a constant force; F_parallel is the component parallel to the object's velocity.
ced_evidence: 3.5.A.4 "instantaneous power delivered to an object by the component of a constant force parallel to the object's velocity"
